meta.description: Time tables for lunar south-pole landing-window work: lunar eclipse dates (NASA catalogue), researcher-DERIVED south-polar solstice/equinox dates, seasonal-shift statements, cycle lengths and constants, and dated analysis epochs / launch periods found in the notes.
meta.coordinate_convention: No coordinates in this file except where quoted in text (decimal degrees, south negative, east-positive). Dates are ISO (YYYY-MM-DD). Eclipse times are Terrestrial (Dynamical) Time of greatest eclipse.
notes: Values copied from research notes of 2026-11-14; not independently validated.

SOLSTICE/EQUINOX DATES ARE NOT PUBLISHED VALUES. They were computed by the researcher (two independent derivations in two notes) from mean lunar-node and solar-longitude formulae and carry "derived_not_published": true. No NASA or peer-reviewed source lists dated south-polar solstices. Verify with SPICE/Horizons sub-solar latitude before use.

The two derivations differ by 0-2 days for the same event and state different uncertainties (about +/-1-2 days vs about +/-5 days); both are kept (type solstice_equinox_cycle_derived and type solstice_list_derived_alt).

Season model used by the researcher: subsolar latitude ~ +1.54 deg x sin(L_sun - Omega), L_sun = Sun's ecliptic longitude, Omega = mean longitude of lunar ascending node (regresses 19.34 deg/yr); southern midsummer at L_sun - Omega = 270 deg, midwinter at 90 deg.

Several cycle lengths (synodic month, draconic month, draconic year, libration amplitude, Sun/Earth angular sizes) are textbook values supplied by the researcher and NOT sourced from a fetched page; they have source_url null and a caveat.
Item 'type' values: lunar_eclipse, lunar_eclipse_later_total, solstice_equinox_cycle_derived, solstice_list_derived_alt, seasonal_statement, cycle_length, launch_period_example, analysis_epoch.

items.statement: South polar illumination conditions exhibit strong seasonal variability and shift approximately 2-3 weeks per year; regions less sensitive to seasonal effects were favoured.
Peak lighting conditions are periodic and shift 2-3 weeks earlier each year, where by 2030 peak solar illumination occurs around the month of August.
items.evidence: primary (NASA slide; text decoded from an obfuscated PDF layer)

items.statement: In 2024 the year begins mid-South Pole summer, with the subsolar latitude near its greatest southern extent; shadows deepen until mid-year (South Pole winter).
In 2022 NASA described south-polar 'summer' as roughly October to March, with some high peaks/ridges getting near-continuous light then.
The Moon has roughly 11 seasonal cycles per 10 Earth years, so the best lighting months slide through the Earth calendar.
Clementine (71 days in early 1994) began imaging 'just after mid-winter for the Moon's southern hemisphere'.
Lighting varies seasonally and can disqualify a large number of nominal HLS missions over a year; for 2026-2027 the best Orion/HLS solutions fell in the winter 2026-2027 (Earth calendar) period.
Area cold enough (<110 K) to trap water grows by a factor of 2.8 in southern winter (4.3 in the north); seasonal change in maximum temperature in seasonally shadowed terrain exceeds 100 K.
items.evidence: primary abstract / search excerpt of Fig. 7

items.statement: Researcher: for a 2028 landing the favourable season is roughly Aug-Dec 2028 (derived solstice 11 Oct 2028); an 'early 2028' landing would fall near the January 2028 equinox heading into winter (worst lighting around 17 Apr 2028). Umbral lunar eclipses cluster at the polar equinoxes (about 87 days before/after each solstice), not in mid-summer.
items.evidence: derived by researcher, not a NASA statement
items.caveat: no source URL in notes

items.statement: Researcher reasoning: the 18.6-year nodal cycle does not change the amplitudes of Sun (+/-1.54 deg) and Earth (about +/-6.7 deg) elevation swings at the pole; it changes the calendar date of the seasons (full circuit every 18.6 years), so lit intervals do not repeat year to year and multi-year statistics should span 18.6 years.
items.caveat: no source URL in notes; no source quantifies year-to-year illumination variation over the cycle

items.name: Lunar rotational obliquity to the ecliptic
items.notes: Max Sun elevation at the poles 1.54 deg (disc centre); max/min subsolar latitude over 1000 years of JPL Horizons ephemerides +/-1.59 deg (Bussey 2010); Sun's apparent latitude range ~3 deg total (SVS 4770).

items.name: Lunar (synodic) day
items.notes: At the equator ~15 d light / ~15 d night (Glaeser); ~14.5/14.5 (NASA white paper).

items.name: Synodic month (Sun azimuth cycle at the pole)
items.caveat: no source URL in notes; textbook value supplied by researcher, not separately sourced

items.name: Draconic month (period of libration in latitude / Earth elevation cycle at the pole)
items.caveat: no source URL in notes; textbook value, not sourced

items.name: Draconic ('eclipse' / lunar seasonal) year
items.notes: Illumination note: '~346.6 days, i.e. 18.6 days shorter than a calendar year'. 365.25 - 346.62 = 18.6 d/yr earlier; 3652.5/346.62 = 10.5 cycles per decade. Beat period 1/(1/27.2122 - 1/29.5306) = 346.6 d (researcher derivation).
items.caveat: no source URL in notes; standard value not confirmed from a fetched primary page

items.name: Lunar nodal precession / nutation cycle
items.notes: NASA average illumination and Earth-visibility maps are averaged hourly over one cycle ('an entire lunar nutation cycle (~18.6 years) with a timestep of one hour'). Node regresses 19.34 deg/yr (researcher's model parameter).

items.name: Libration in latitude: amplitude and period
items.value: about +/-6.7 deg (5.15 deg orbit inclination + 1.54 deg obliquity); period = draconic month 27.21 d
items.notes: Earth's disc ~1.9 deg (angular radius ~0.95 deg); Sun angular radius ~0.27 deg.
items.caveat: no source URL in notes; textbook values, not sourced; no fetched source states the libration amplitude or exact up/down period of Earth

items.name: Earth visibility cycle at near-pole sites
items.value: ~4-week cycle: visible ~2 weeks, not visible ~2 weeks; DTE windows ~14 days

items.name: NRHO period (legacy staging orbit; 9:2 synodic resonance)
items.notes: 365.25 / 6.562 = 55.7 revs per year (researcher arithmetic); reference trajectory 2 Jan 2020 - 11 Feb 2035.

items.name: Lunar Pathfinder orbit period
items.caveat: 2023 slides via search excerpt.

items.name: Queqiao-2 orbit period
items.value: 24 h planned (observed 26.18 h per amateur tracking); 12 h orbit planned later
items.caveat: secondary source

items.name: LROC WAC polar illumination campaign ('one lunar year')
items.value: 15 February 2010 to 5 February 2011; 3,807 south-pole images, repeat approximately every 2 hours

items.name: Solar cycle 25 phase
items.value: peaked around 2024, declining toward a minimum around ~2031; ~24-48 h warning of solar particle events
items.caveat: weak, secondary sourcing; no NASA date criterion based on solar-cycle phase found

items.notes: ~2 weeks of opportunities then ~2 weeks without.

items.name: Chang'e-7 launch window 2026 (missed)
items.notes: Postponed 23 Aug 2026; now 2027 at the earliest. Researcher: a 2027 retry would need the season around the derived solstice of 30 Oct 2027.
